stem.text: The function f gives the height, in meters, of a drone above the ground at time x seconds. The function f is differentiable for all x except \( x = 4 \), where it has a jump discontinuity. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 1 < c < 7 \), such that \( f'(c) = 4 \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = 4 \), f is not continuous at \( x = 4 \), which lies in \( \left[1, 7\right] \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[1, 7\right] \) is \( \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = \frac{20 - (-4)}{6} = 4 \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[1, 7\right] \) and differentiable on \( (1, 7) \), but f is not continuous at \( x = 4 \), which lies in \( \left[1, 7\right] \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = 4 \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = 4 \), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be continuous on \( \left[1, 7\right] \).
options.derivation: the Intermediate Value Theorem cited for a claim about the derivative

options.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = 4 \), f is not continuous at \( x = 4 \), which lies in \( \left[1, 7\right] \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.
Yes. Since \( \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = 4 \), there is a c with \( 1 < c < 7 \) and \( f'(c) = 4 \), because an average rate of change is always reached by the derivative.
options.derivation: existence asserted from the arithmetic alone, with no theorem named and no check that one applies

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(7) - f(1)}{7 - 1} = 4 \), the Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be differentiable on \( (1, 7) \).
options.derivation: the Mean Value Theorem applied without checking its hypotheses, which fail at x = 4
